sections.heading: A public beginning, not a finished theory
paragraphs: This first edition opens a small part of an ongoing body of work. Some pages define a working concept. Others pose a question or connect existing research. Their status is visible so a useful idea does not need to pretend it is a final conclusion.
The full arguments remain in their project repositories. The Wiki holds shared identities and relationships. This site is the readable entrance, not a replacement for either.

sections.heading: For a different kind of work
paragraphs: Root Sequence investigates questions and patterns. Coherent World explores possible arrangements and their interactions. No One Noticed turns that design space into lives, uncertainty, conflict, and consequence. The Museum of Ordinary Life is a separate real archive, not an annex of the fiction.
Practical projects can test an assumption without proving an entire speculative world. A story can reveal a question without counting as evidence that its imagined solution works.

sections.heading: For a thought that needs somewhere to go
paragraphs: The existing RS? convention is the logical intake path: capture once, search existing work, choose a canonical home, and add useful relationships. A capture is not automatic publication. We are connecting that path to the public work rather than creating another inbox.

sections.heading: How to read a Seed
paragraphs: Seed describes development, not truth. A short working question can be a Seed; a polished claim can still be wrong. Each guide separately describes its kind, epistemic status, dates, and sources.

These are reader-facing interpretations, not a comprehensive literature review. Factual case studies and institutional comparisons will need dated evidence and explicit uncertainties before they are added.

pages.title: Coherence as a direction
pages.description: What would it mean to make conditions more coherent without claiming to have designed a final, perfect world?

sections.heading: A working use of the word
paragraphs: Here, coherence is an invitation to examine how parts fit together: whether a system can support its stated purposes without hiding incompatible dependencies, unacknowledged burdens, or unresolved consequences. This is a working design lens, not a single proven measure for society.

Increasing coherence does not require everybody to become alike. Different practices, priorities, and representations may be appropriate in different places. A quiet disagreement is not automatically a defect; apparent agreement is not automatically evidence of a well-functioning system.

sections.heading: Conditions before conclusions
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical transport service that appears efficient only because its timetable assumes a level of mobility that some passengers do not have. The design question is not simply how to make the timetable faster. It is what conditions allow people to reach what they need, how those conditions differ, and which burdens the timetable leaves out.

The practical task is therefore iterative: identify a mismatch, understand whom it affects, make a bounded change, inspect the effects, and retain the ability to correct it. A system can improve along one dimension while deteriorating along another. Calling the result coherent should never conceal that tradeoff.

sections.heading: What remains open
paragraphs: Whose purposes count? Which effects are within the boundary of the assessment? What evidence would show that a claimed improvement merely moved a burden elsewhere? How can disagreement remain legible? These questions belong inside the method, not in a footnote after success has been declared.

For Coherent World, this supports a direction of travel rather than a perfected end-state. For No One Noticed, it leaves room for consequences that exceed the explanation of whoever designed the intervention.

pages.epistemic_status: Working proposal; not a validated metric

pages.title: Abandoned futures
pages.description: An investigation into possibilities that were imagined, attempted, interrupted, or overlooked—not a claim that every discarded idea deserved to survive.

sections.heading: A motif is a beginning
paragraphs: The project carries a recurring motif: we do not have to imagine every future from nothing. But a memorable line is not a historical finding. Each candidate needs its own evidence, its own context, and a clear account of what is being proposed for the present.

The useful first move is to separate several possibilities: something was technically unworkable; it met a different need; its costs were displaced onto others; it was prevented from developing; or the evidence is simply too thin to tell. Those explanations should not be collapsed into a single comforting story.

sections.heading: A candidate record
paragraphs: For an abandoned-future entry, ask what was actually proposed, who participated, what evidence survives, why it stopped, and which explanation is disputed. Then ask what would have to change for a related idea to work now. Describe beneficiaries and burdens separately.

A photograph of an attractive design cannot establish that it was accessible or maintainable. An old proposal cannot establish that present-day communities would choose it. A surviving example can expose a possibility without proving that the same arrangement transfers to another setting.

sections.heading: Recovery without nostalgia
paragraphs: The point is not to replace inevitability about the present with inevitability about a preferred future. It is to make the choice space more inspectable. Some possibilities may be worth developing; others may be warnings, partial lessons, or ideas whose useful life has ended.

In the fiction, an imagined recovery can be explored through a changed routine or an unexpected absence. Outside the fiction, the claim remains a research task. The distinction matters: a compelling scene is not the missing case study.

pages.epistemic_status: Research questions; no case findings claimed

pages.title: Legible systems
pages.description: A system can be simple to use without being required to remain mysterious.

sections.heading: Different depths, one system
paragraphs: The existing Legible Systems foundation proposes progressive access to understanding: use a system, configure it, inspect it, modify it, repair it, and learn why it works. Not everyone must travel the entire path. The important design question is whether the path remains available.

An ordinary user should not need to become a specialist before receiving a useful explanation. A specialist should not lose access to the technical trace because the default interface is simplified. Those are complementary requirements, not opposing audiences to choose between.

sections.heading: Explanation first; trace underneath
paragraphs: Imagine a failed file transfer. The first layer explains what happened, whether the original is safe, and what action is available. A deeper layer exposes the exact error, time, destination, and relevant log. The explanation does not replace the evidence, and the evidence does not excuse an incomprehensible explanation.

The same approach can guide physical objects, shared procedures, and tools. Start with the function and the person's immediate question. Then make the dependencies, controls, and repair path available without requiring knowledge that the system could have revealed itself.

sections.heading: Legibility is not universal exposure
paragraphs: Making a system understandable does not require making people's private information visible. Explain the mechanism, scope of authority, and available remedy while preserving appropriate boundaries around the people involved.

For this website, the practical test is modest: can a visitor tell what a page is, how developed it is, where it came from, and where to continue? The canonical research remains linked below; this guide is an entrance, not a replacement.

pages.title: Resilience and graceful degradation
pages.description: When the preferred mechanism disappears, what capability disappears with it?

sections.heading: Protect the purpose
paragraphs: The project's resilience note distinguishes a component from the capability it supports. Preserving a particular interface is not the same as preserving the ability to communicate, navigate, obtain help, or repair a problem.

Consider a hypothetical meeting service whose live interface stops working. A locally saved location and a known human contact may preserve the essential task. The fallback is not identical to the original service, and it may be less convenient. What matters is whether a useful capability survives within an honest, known set of limits.

sections.heading: A fallback needs its own explanation
paragraphs: Calling something a backup leaves several questions unanswered. Does it depend on the same account, network, power source, or person as the primary system? Can the people who need it find and use it? Is it maintained? What is lost when it is used? Has the transition actually been tested?

A staffed desk is not automatically accessible. A printed instruction is not automatically understandable. An alternate method can introduce its own exclusions or failure modes. Resilience work should compare the paths rather than romanticize the older or simpler one.

sections.heading: Practice on this project
paragraphs: This first website is being built as static files with relative internal links, an edition archive, and a manifest of file hashes. These choices make the output easier to inspect and move. They do not provide an independent backup or prove long-term preservation.

The remaining practical work includes checking the live host, keeping an independent copy, documenting recovery, and testing that a reader can still reach the material after an ordinary failure. A successful local build is the beginning of that evidence, not its substitute.

pages.title: Imagination and prediction
pages.description: What could be possible is a different question from what is likely to happen.

sections.heading: Two different tasks
paragraphs: For this project, prediction asks what outcomes follow under a specified set of assumptions. Imagination asks what arrangements or events might become thinkable when some of those assumptions change. This distinction is useful for organizing work; it is not a claim that people or machines always perform either task in a pure form.

A forecast can be useful and still leave an important assumption unexplored. An imaginative proposal can expand the question and still be infeasible, undesirable, or poorly supported. Neither activity replaces the other.

sections.heading: Do not smuggle a forecast into a scene
paragraphs: Suppose a fictional service eliminates a familiar inconvenience. The scene can make a possibility tangible: how someone uses the time, what they distrust, or which relationship changes. It cannot establish the engineering feasibility or social acceptance of the service.

The next research step is to identify what the scene assumed. Which resources exist? Who maintains the service? How can somebody refuse it? Which effects appear only after repeated use? An appealing answer may reveal a hidden cost; an apparent obstacle may turn out to depend on an assumption worth examining.

sections.heading: A two-way path
paragraphs: Use research to expose the constraints of an imagined world. Use imagined situations to expose questions the research has not yet asked. Keep the provenance and uncertainty visible as material travels between them.

No One Noticed does not need to predict how artificial intelligence will develop in order to be worth writing. Its task can be to explore a consequential possibility without presenting that possibility as an inevitable rescue, an inevitable catastrophe, or a finished explanation of the future.

pages.title: Connected, not contained.
pages.description: One body of work, several distinct jobs. This is a selected orientation map; the existing Wiki remains the identity and relationship layer.

sections.heading: Research, possibility, experience
paragraphs: Root Sequence investigates. Coherent World explores system designs. No One Noticed turns that design space into experience. These relationships run in both directions: a fictional consequence can uncover a research question, and research can force a scene to change.
Coherent World does not need a separate website to begin contributing. The coherent.world domain is not treated here as a purchased or deployed dependency.

sections.heading: Real-world work remains real
paragraphs: The Museum of Ordinary Life is an autonomous archive. Its real contributors, records, permissions, and governance do not become fictional assets because a Museum also appears in the story. Any fictional document on the story site must be labeled as invented.
Community Infrastructure and Coherent Computing are distinct design and implementation tracks. Their inclusion here is not a claim that a pilot is running or an operating system has shipped.

pages.title: An unfinished work should say how it is unfinished.
pages.description: Development, evidence, fictional canon, and permission to publish are different things.

sections.heading: Maturity
paragraphs: Seed means an idea is worth preserving and developing. Growing means it has received more structure, connections, and scrutiny. Established means it is a relatively mature project reference. None of these labels makes a claim true, permanent, or universally applicable.

sections.heading: Evidence and canon
paragraphs: A research question is not a finding. A design proposal is not a deployed service. A fictional document is not a real record. A canon label describes its standing inside a story, not whether it is a prescription for the real world.
Each page separately identifies its kind, epistemic status, dates, sources, and—where relevant—canon status. These reading guides do not silently change the status of their source documents.

sections.heading: Publication
paragraphs: Public repositories are public even when a branch or page is called a draft. Private story material is therefore staged in the private story repository, not hidden behind a label in a public repository.

The site builder creates a preview by default. A release build requires a separate approval record matching the exact source files. Search-engine exclusion on a preview is a courtesy, not an access-control mechanism.

sections.heading: Credits and continuity
paragraphs: Root Sequence is a project by Rae Lovejoy. These initial reader-facing guides and the publishing scaffold were prepared with AI assistance from the project's existing material and current planning discussion.
The canonical research, history, and project relationships remain in the linked repositories and Wiki. The static edition archive is a portable copy, not a guarantee that the work can never be lost.
